summary: Describes the Alternate-Marking technique, which measures packet loss, delay, and jitter on live traffic by periodically flipping a marking bit in packets so that counts can be compared between measurement points. It can work with different protocols and can be passive or hybrid. It obsoletes RFC 8321.

eli5.summary: Cars on a road get painted red for a while, then blue. By counting red and blue cars at two spots, you can tell if any went missing or got slow.

questions: how to measure packet loss on live traffic
how to measure network delay and jitter passively
how to measure one way delay with marking bits
what is the alternate marking guard band
subtitle: Measure packet loss, delay and jitter on live traffic by flipping a marking bit in packet headers.

tldr.problem: Operators need to measure packet loss, delay and jitter on real traffic. Sequence numbers are hard to use on live traffic, and plain counters at two points cannot be compared unless they cover exactly the same packets.
tldr.mechanism: Packets of a flow are colored with a marking bit that changes on a fixed timer, which splits the flow into blocks. Each measurement point counts and timestamps packets per color, and the results for the same block are compared.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 8321 with clarified wording and one-flag and two-flag recommendations, and it MUST only be applied within a controlled domain.

today: RFC 9341 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2022. It obsoletes RFC 8321, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Alternate Marking
sections.content:
Service Provider networks carry traffic that is sensitive to packet loss, delay and jitter, so they need ways to monitor performance. RFC 7799 defines Active, Passive and Hybrid methods of measurement. The Alternate-Marking Method is potentially applicable to any packet-based traffic, point-to-point unicast and multicast, including Ethernet, IP and MPLS. It primarily addresses packet loss but extends to one-way and two-way delay and delay variation.

Under the RFC 7799 classification it can be considered Passive or Hybrid, and the text calls it Hybrid Type I because changing marking bits at the domain edges counts as modifying the stream of interest. This is a methodology document: how counters and timestamps are transmitted is out of scope.

It obsoletes RFC 8321. The changes are backward compatible and introduce no new technique. They add recommendations for one or two available flag bits, improve the structure, remove experimental wording, and expand synchronization, timing, fragmentation and marked versus unmarked traffic.
sections.eli5: It is a way to check how well a road works by looking at the traffic that is already there, without sending special test cars.

sections.title: The Idea: Color the Packets
sections.content:
Numbering every packet would let a router spot a missing one, but it needs a sequence number in each packet and real-time extraction, which can be hard on live traffic. Counting packets at both ends and comparing is simpler, but both counters must cover exactly the same packets. Inserting special delimiter packets has its own limits: it needs extra packets and is vulnerable to out-of-order reception.

Alternate marking instead marks the packets themselves. Packets in the same block share a notional color, and consecutive blocks have different colors. Each color change acts as an auto-synchronization signal. By enabling measurement on several interfaces, an operator can do link, node or end-to-end monitoring and isolate the faulty element.
sections.eli5: Instead of stopping the cars to count them, you paint them red for a while and then blue. Everyone along the road knows which batch they are counting.

sections.title: Measuring Packet Loss
sections.content:
Two colors are enough. When the color changes, the previous block ends and a new one begins. Using a fixed timer to create blocks is REQUIRED. Switching after a fixed number of packets is an additional possibility, but its detailed specification is out of scope.

For a link between routers R1 and R2, R1 keeps two egress counters, one per color, and R2 keeps two ingress counters. When a block of color A ends, comparing the A counters on R1 and R2 gives the loss within that block, and similarly for B. Because some packets can arrive out of order, it is preferable not to read the counter right after the switch; a safe choice is to wait L/2 time units, where L is the block duration.

The flow-based strategy, which colors only specified flows, is REQUIRED. For end-to-end monitoring it is enough to enable monitoring on the first-hop and last-hop routers, and intermediate nodes are not involved. The link-based strategy measures all traffic on a link-by-link basis.
sections.eli5: If 100 red cars enter the road and only 98 leave, two went missing. You compare the counts for one color at a time.

sections.title: Delay and Jitter
sections.content:
The same principle yields one-way delay, and adding the delays of both directions gives the two-way delay. With Single Marking, a device stores the timestamp of the first packet of each new block, and comparing it with the same packet's timestamp on a second router gives the delay. Clocks MUST be in sync, and the measurement is valid only if no packet loss or misordering happens. A mean delay variant averages arrival times over a block and is robust to reordering, but gives only one value per block and no minimum, maximum or median.

With Double Marking, a first marking creates the alternating flow and a second marking selects packets for delay measurement. The selected packets must be spaced far enough apart to avoid reordering, and an efficient, robust mode is to choose a single double-marked packet per block. The text advises avoiding the plain range (maximum minus minimum) and points to the 99.9th percentile as more useful.

Inter-arrival jitter is derived from the delay variation of consecutive samples, using the first packet of each block (Single Marking) or the second-marked packets (Double Marking).
sections.eli5: To see how long the trip takes, you note when one special car left and when it arrived. Using one special car per batch avoids mix-ups when cars overtake each other.

sections.title: Marking, Counting and Collecting
sections.content:
Coloring is done by setting flags in the packet header and changing the value periodically. Which field to use is out of scope. For flow-based measurement, selection rules such as header fields define the flow. A single coloring node is easier to manage, and coloring as close to the source as possible allows end-to-end measurement. For link-based measurement every hop re-colors the traffic, and the color need not match across links. Two counters per flow and per monitored interface are needed.

Nodes only have their own samples, so counters and timestamps must be collected and correlated. This can be centralized, with a Network Management System receiving pushed data or polling routers, or distributed using a protocol, for example by extending TWAMP or OWAMP. An implementation MAY use a Block Number (BN) attached to every report so that counts for the same block can be matched, which assumes time-synchronized nodes.

For fragmentation, marking nodes MUST mark all fragments if flag bits exist, and nodes that fragment inside the domain SHOULD ensure only one fragment carries the marking bit. Measurement points SHOULD ignore unmarked fragments and count marked ones as full packets.
sections.eli5: Each counting post writes down its numbers and sends them to a central office, which lines up the notes for the same batch and compares them.

sections.title: Synchronization and Timing
sections.content:
Color switching is the reference for all measurement points. They must be synchronized to the same clock reference with adequate accuracy so every device matches the marking bit to the correct block. Packet reordering, for example from equal-cost multipath, also matters. If the block is large enough, reordering happens only at the edge of adjacent blocks.

Assume clocks agree within +/- A/2, so any two differ by at most A. The guard band d is the clock accuracy plus the average network delay plus three standard deviations of the delay. The available counting interval is L - 2d, which must be greater than zero. The condition d < L/2 MUST be satisfied, and packet counters and double-marked packets MUST be taken within that interval. A longer block relaxes the synchronization requirement, but makes measurements less frequent.
sections.eli5: All the counters need clocks that agree closely. You also leave a safety gap around each color change, so late cars do not get counted in the wrong batch.

sections.title: One Flag or Two
sections.content:
The number of available flag bits decides the method. With one flag, packet loss MUST be measured as in Section 3.1 and delay MUST use Single Marking, with mean delay as an optional extra that costs more computation. With two flags, loss is the same and delay MUST use Double Marking, and Single Marking MAY also be combined with it for a more robust data set.

Other factors are the marking period, which sets measurement frequency but is limited by the timing rule, the kind of data needed, and the computational resources at the measurement points. Measurement points can learn whether measurement is active from whether the dedicated protocol extension is present in the packets.

RFC 9342 is referenced for generalizing the coloring and counting to multipoint-to-multipoint flows.
sections.eli5: If you only have one paint color switch, you can count cars and time one car per batch. With two, you can time a few chosen cars very precisely too.

sections.title: Controlled Domains and Security
sections.content:
For security reasons the method MUST only be applied to a controlled domain: a managed network that enforces policies at its boundaries to discard undesired external packets entering and to check internal packets leaving. Externally marked packets must be checked and filtered or cleared, because an outside attacker could send marked packets.

The measurements are Passive, so no new packets are injected. Because the marking bits are the only information exchanged between devices, eavesdropping on data traffic does not reveal network performance. Threats include routers altering marks, injected traffic, and delay attacks: an on-path attacker could delay only the delay-colored packets, or attack the time protocol. Channels that report statistics back MUST be secured. The marking could in theory serve as a covert channel, but with a very low data rate. The RFC has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: The paint trick only works if everyone on the road follows the rules, so it is used only inside a network that one team controls.
